screens.title: Securing Data Pipelines and Endpoints
screens.narratorSegment: In this lesson you'll learn how to secure every stage of a data pipeline in Azure. We take a layered approach: start with network isolation using Virtual Networks and Private Endpoints, add traffic controls with Network Security Groups and Azure Firewall, and then enforce identity, secrets, and encryption with Azure Active Directory, RBAC, Managed Identities, and Key Vault. You will see concrete configuration steps for creating a Private Endpoint to an ADLS Gen2 account and for granting a managed identity least-privilege access to a specific container. A common pitfall is enabling Private Link but forgetting to integrate DNS or to disable public access; we'll highlight those traps and how to avoid them. Understanding these controls matters because pipelines often handle sensitive or regulated data; a misconfigured endpoint or overly broad role assignment is where breaches start. As you follow the walkthrough, think about the difference between network-level isolation and identity-based controls, and how they work together to keep data private and auditable. By the end you should be able to design a pipeline that avoids public internet exposure and follows least-privilege principles.

screens.title: Azure Virtual Network (VNet) — logical isolation
screens.narratorSegment: A Virtual Network, or VNet, is the primary mechanism for isolating Azure resources inside a private IP space. When you provision compute for data processing—like a self-hosted integration runtime or a VNet-injected Databricks cluster—placing that compute in a VNet prevents its management interfaces and data paths from being directly exposed to the public internet. VNets allow you to define address ranges, subnets, and route tables so you control how traffic flows. A concrete example: deploy a self-hosted integration runtime into a subnet that also contains a jump box with restricted SSH access; then use a VPN Gateway to connect your on-premises network privately. A common misconception is thinking VNets alone are sufficient. VNets provide isolation but you still need NSGs, firewall rules, and private endpoints to control and limit traffic to specific ports and services. The core takeaway is that VNets are the scaffold for secure pipelines; they constrain network reachability so identity and encryption controls can be effective. Consider: where in your design do you need to stop public egress, and which subnets should hold your managed and unmanaged compute?

content.html:
Core Concept

Virtual Network (VNet)

A VNet provides logical isolation and private IP addressing for Azure resources used by your pipeline.

Define address space and subnets
Place compute (SHIR, Databricks) inside a VNet
Use VPN or ExpressRoute for private on-prem connectivity
Key Takeaway

VNets form the network boundary; they must be paired with traffic controls and identity policies.

Illustrative architecture
Subnet: Processing
Databricks (VNet-injected)
Private IPs, no public exposure. Uses VNet routes and NSGs to limit outbound services.
Subnet: Management
Jump Box / Bastion
Restricted SSH access from a known admin IP; used to manage resources without opening them publicly.
Design note: Use route tables to control egress and plan which subnets can reach Private Endpoints or NAT gateways.

screens.title: Network Security Groups (NSGs) — filtering traffic
screens.narratorSegment: Network Security Groups are the virtual firewall you attach to subnets or individual NICs to allow or deny traffic based on source or destination IP, port, and protocol. They are stateful and rule-ordered; the first matching rule takes effect. A typical configuration allows management traffic only from a jump box IP and allows outbound connections to required Azure service endpoints. For example, you might permit inbound TCP port 22 only from your admin jump box, and permit outbound HTTPS to storage endpoints. A common error is relying solely on NSGs without a centralized firewall; NSGs are effective for subnet-level controls but they do not provide FQDN filtering or threat intelligence. Use NSGs for low-latency packet filtering and Azure Firewall when you need central policy, FQDN controls, or cross-VNet rules. When you design rules, document the justification and expiration for any wide-open rules; temporary allowances often become permanent if not audited. Consider how NSGs and route tables interact, and test rules in a staging VNet before applying to production. Network Security Groups (NSGs) — filtering traffic means use nsgs for targeted allow/deny controls and pair them with a centralized firewall when you need fqdn filtering or policy across vnets.. In practical terms, how nsgs enforce subnet- and vm-level rules. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Process Flow

Network Security Groups

NSGs filter traffic by source/destination, port and protocol. Attach them at subnet or NIC level.

Example Rule Set
  • Allow inbound TCP 22 from AdminJumpBoxIP
  • Deny inbound all other SSH
  • Allow outbound TCP 443 to storage endpoints
Common mistake: leaving a broad inbound rule without expiration or review.
Key Takeaway

Document and audit NSG rules, and prefer narrow allow rules with defined owners.

Visual: NSG scope & effect
Attached to Subnet
Subnet-level policies apply to all NICs inside
Good for broad segmentation like 'processing' vs 'management'.
Attached to NIC
NIC-level policies override for specific VMs
Useful for exceptions or strict host-level controls.

screens.title: Azure Firewall vs NSGs
screens.narratorSegment: Azure Firewall and NSGs complement each other but serve different needs. NSGs are efficient, low-latency packet filters used for subnet- or NIC-level access controls. They are rule-ordered and ideal for basic allow/deny scenarios. Azure Firewall is a managed, stateful, cloud firewall service that centralizes traffic policy across VNets and supports features NSGs do not: FQDN filtering, threat intelligence, and application rules that operate at the domain level. A practical design is to use NSGs to implement fast, layered filtering near compute and use Azure Firewall as a central enforcement point for egress policies and cross-VNet controls. For sensitive pipelines, Azure Firewall can block access to known malicious domains and allow lists of storage FQDNs, which NSGs cannot. A common misconception is to replace NSGs with Firewall entirely; instead, combine them: NSGs for local enforcement and Firewall for centralized policy and logging. Ask yourself: do you need domain-level control and threat intelligence, or only simple IP/port filtering? That question guides whether to add Firewall to your architecture. Azure Firewall vs NSGs means pair nsgs for local filtering with azure firewall for centralized, fqdn-aware egress control and threat intelligence.. In practical terms, when to use a centralized firewall and when nsgs are enough. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Comparison

NSG: low-latency packet filter

  • Subnet or NIC scope
  • IP/port/protocol rules
  • Stateful, rule-ordered
Best for fast, local segmentation and host-level exceptions.
Comparison

Azure Firewall: managed, centralized

  • FQDN and application filtering
  • Threat intelligence & logging
  • Policy across VNets
Best for egress control, domain allow-lists, and centralized monitoring.
Key Takeaway

Use both: NSGs for local filtering and Azure Firewall for centralized, domain-aware egress and threat controls.

screens.title: Azure Private Link and Private Endpoints
screens.narratorSegment: Azure Private Link enables private connectivity to PaaS services by presenting a Private Endpoint inside your VNet. That endpoint is a network interface assigned a private IP from your subnet, and it maps to the PaaS resource. The result: traffic flows over the Azure backbone and does not traverse the public internet. For data services like ADLS Gen2 or Azure S Q L, this means your data factory or Databricks cluster can access storage without hitting public endpoints. A concrete example is creating a Private Endpoint targeting the 'blob' or 'dfs' sub-resource of a storage account; once created and DNS is correctly configured, the storage FQDN resolves to the private IP. Common mistakes include leaving public access enabled after adding Private Link or failing to integrate a private DNS zone so resolution still returns public addresses. The important design idea is that Private Link removes exposure while preserving the managed PaaS experience. Think about how private endpoints affect peering, routing, and DNS when you plan subnet placement. Azure Private Link and Private Endpoints means private endpoints provide private ips for paas services so traffic stays on the azure backbone; dns integration is essential.. In practical terms, bringing paas services into your vnet with private ips. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition

Private Link & Private Endpoint

A Private Endpoint is a NIC with a private IP in your VNet that connects privately to a PaaS resource.

Eliminates exposure to public internet
Maintains PaaS management while providing private connectivity
Requires DNS integration to resolve service names to private IPs
Concrete example
Configure a Private Endpoint for an ADLS Gen2 storage account and choose the 'blob' or 'dfs' target sub-resource. Integrate with the privatelink DNS zone so that calls to your storage account name return the private address.
Common mistake: forgetting to disable public access after adding a private endpoint results in dual-access paths and potential data exposure.
Key Takeaway

Private Endpoints keep pipeline traffic on the private Azure backbone; confirm DNS to avoid accidental public resolution.

screens.title: Walkthrough: Create a Private Endpoint for ADLS Gen2 (conceptual)
screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough describes the conceptual steps to create a Private Endpoint for an ADLS Gen2 storage account. Follow these steps in your portal when you're ready. First, open the storage account and navigate to Networking, then choose Private Endpoint connections and add a new private endpoint. In Basics, pick subscription, resource group, name and region matching your VNet. Under Resource, select 'Connect to an Azure resource in my directory', set Resource type to Microsoft. Storage/storageAccounts, choose your storage account and target sub-resource 'blob' or 'dfs'. For Virtual Network, select the VNet and subnet where the endpoint's private IP will reside. The crucial DNS option is 'Integrate with private DNS zone' — set this to Yes to automatically create or link a privatelink DNS zone so your storage name resolves privately. Finally, review and create. A frequent misconception is proceeding without checking region and DNS; mismatched regions or missing private DNS integration will leave traffic resolving to public IPs. Remember: do not create a production endpoint without a plan for testing and cost review. content.html:
Process Flow

Create Private Endpoint (Conceptual Steps)

1. In the Storage Account, open Networking → Private endpoint connections
2. Click + Private endpoint
3. Basics: select subscription, resource group, name, region (match VNet)
4. Resource: Connect to an Azure resource in my directory
   - Resource type: Microsoft.Storage/storageAccounts
   - Resource: select your ADLS Gen2 account
   - Target sub-resource: blob (or dfs for ADLS Gen2)
5. Virtual Network: choose VNet and Subnet for the private IP
6. DNS: Integrate with private DNS zone → Yes
7. Review + create

IMPORTANT: Do not create in production without verification. Check region and DNS settings to avoid public fallback.
Pro tip: When you enable DNS integration the privatelink zone will map the storage FQDN to the private IP automatically, avoiding manual host records.
Key Takeaway

The target sub-resource and DNS integration choices determine whether the storage account is actually reachable over the private backbone.

screens.title: Private DNS Zones and common DNS pitfalls
screens.narratorSegment: When you create a Private Endpoint, DNS is the step that makes private connectivity usable. Private Link typically pairs a private endpoint with a private DNS zone such as privatelink. blob. core. windows. net. If you accept automatic integration, Azure will create or link the zone and add the appropriate A record so your storage account name resolves to the private IP. If you do not integrate DNS, clients inside your VNet will continue to see the public IP for the service and traffic will route through the public internet. A common pitfall is creating the Private Endpoint but failing to update DNS for peered VNets or on-premises resolver settings, leaving parts of the network still resolving publicly. For hybrid setups you may need conditional forwarders or DNS forwarding rules to ensure on-premises names resolve to private addresses. Always test resolution from the intended client host and verify that the fully qualified storage name maps to a private IP before disabling public access. Private DNS Zones and common DNS pitfalls means private endpoint creation is incomplete without private dns integration and resolver configuration for peered or on-prem clients.. In practical terms, ensure service names resolve to private ips inside your vnet. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

content.html:
Definition

Private DNS zones

A private DNS zone maps service FQDNs to private IPs inside VNets so Private Endpoints are reachable without public resolution.

Common zone: privatelink.blob.core.windows.net
Automatic integration creates the record mapping the storage name to the private IP
For peered VNets or on-prem, configure DNS forwarding or link the private zone
Checklist & common mistakes
  • Does storage name resolve to private IP from target host?
  • Are private DNS zones linked to all VNets that need access?
  • Have you configured on-prem DNS forwarding if hybrid clients require access?
Pitfall: Disabling public access before DNS is validated causes outages.
Key Takeaway

Validate DNS resolution from each client location before switching off public endpoints.

screens.title: Identity and access: Azure AD, Managed Identities, and RBAC
screens.narratorSegment: Identity is the control plane that complements network isolation. Azure Active Directory is the identity provider for users, groups, service principals, and managed identities. AAD, Managed Identities & RBAC

Use AAD identities and RBAC to grant permissions with the narrowest necessary scope and prefer managed identities for services.

Example: Storage Blob Data Contributor at container scope

screens.narratorSegment: This walkthrough explains how to grant a managed identity permission to a specific ADLS Gen2 container following the principle of least privilege. Start in the storage account: open Data storage and select Containers. Choose the target container, then open Access control (IAM). Assign Storage Blob Data Contributor to a Managed Identity

1. Storage Account → Data storage → Containers
2. Open target container → Access control (IAM)

screens.title: Encryption: at rest and in transit
screens.narratorSegment: Encryption is a required layer of protection. Most Azure data services encrypt data at rest by default using Microsoft-managed keys. For stronger control, you can enable customer-managed keys stored in Azure Key Vault, which gives you lifecycle control over rotation and revocation. Encryption in transit is provided via TLS/SSL for communications to public endpoints; when you use Private Link, traffic still remains encrypted and stays on the Azure backbone. A concrete pattern: enable CMK for your ADLS Gen2 account so you can rotate keys with Key Vault while auditing key usage. A common misconception is that encryption alone prevents unauthorized reads; it prevents exposure but you still need network and identity controls so only authorized principals get access and keys cannot be misused. Remember to audit key and secret usage and plan key rotation. Finally, ensure that any on-prem or custom components use strong TLS configurations and that secrets are retrieved from Key Vault rather than being embedded in application configuration. Encryption: at rest and in transit means use encryption at rest (cmk if needed) and tls in transit, and pair encryption with access controls and audit processes.. Encryption at Rest

Services default to Microsoft-managed keys. Use customer-managed keys in Key Vault for lifecycle control when required.

Benefit: rotate, revoke, and audit key usage under your control.
Definition

Encryption in Transit

Use TLS/SSL for client-service communication. Private Link keeps traffic on the Azure backbone while maintaining encryption.

Benefit: avoids public exposure and preserves encrypted channels inside Azure.
Key Takeaway

Encryption is necessary but not sufficient; combine with network and identity controls and audit keys and secrets regularly.

fullNarratorScript:
In this lesson you'll learn how to secure every stage of a data pipeline in Azure. We take a layered approach: start with network isolation using Virtual Networks and Private Endpoints, add traffic controls with Network Security Groups and Azure Firewall, and then enforce identity, secrets, and encryption with Azure Active Directory, RBAC, Managed Identities, and Key Vault. You will see concrete configuration steps for creating a Private Endpoint to an ADLS Gen2 account and for granting a managed identity least-privilege access to a specific container. A common pitfall is enabling Private Link but forgetting to integrate DNS or to disable public access; we'll highlight those traps and how to avoid them. Understanding these controls matters because pipelines often handle sensitive or regulated data; a misconfigured endpoint or overly broad role assignment is where breaches start. As you follow the walkthrough, think about the difference between network-level isolation and identity-based controls, and how they work together to keep data private and auditable. By the end you should be able to design a pipeline that avoids public internet exposure and follows least-privilege principles.

By the end of these lessons you'll be able to design and implement core network and access controls that protect Azure data services. First, you'll understand how VNets create logical isolation and how to place data processing workloads inside a VNet to avoid public exposure. Second, you'll configure Network Security Groups and Azure Firewall to enforce inbound and outbound policies that limit where data can flow. Third, you'll implement Azure Private Link and Private Endpoints so PaaS services such as ADLS Gen2 are reachable only over private IPs. Fourth, you'll apply Azure Active Directory and Role-Based Access Control to grant least-privilege permissions to identities and managed services. For each objective you'll see why it matters, a concrete configuration pattern, and a common mistake to avoid. These skills are essential for protecting sensitive pipelines and meeting compliance and auditing requirements in production systems.

These additional objectives prepare you for hands-on configuration and operational hygiene. You will learn to enable customer-managed keys for services that support CMK to control key lifecycle and rotation. You will practice configuring Private DNS zones so private endpoints resolve correctly inside your VNet, avoiding the common misconfiguration where DNS still points to public endpoints. You will also learn to audit access logs and rotate keys and secrets regularly, using Key Vault as a central secrets store. Finally, you'll gain practical experience assigning the Storage Blob Data Contributor role at a container scope to adhere to least privilege. Each objective includes a short walkthrough and a checklist you can use to verify the configuration in production. These skills reduce both exposure and operational risk, and they directly support compliance and incident response readiness.

A Virtual Network, or VNet, is the primary mechanism for isolating Azure resources inside a private IP space. When you provision compute for data processing—like a self-hosted integration runtime or a VNet-injected Databricks cluster—placing that compute in a VNet prevents its management interfaces and data paths from being directly exposed to the public internet. VNets allow you to define address ranges, subnets, and route tables so you control how traffic flows. A concrete example: deploy a self-hosted integration runtime into a subnet that also contains a jump box with restricted SSH access; then use a VPN Gateway to connect your on-premises network privately. A common misconception is thinking VNets alone are sufficient. VNets provide isolation but you still need NSGs, firewall rules, and private endpoints to control and limit traffic to specific ports and services. The core takeaway is that VNets are the scaffold for secure pipelines; they constrain network reachability so identity and encryption controls can be effective. Consider: where in your design do you need to stop public egress, and which subnets should hold your managed and unmanaged compute?

Network Security Groups are the virtual firewall you attach to subnets or individual NICs to allow or deny traffic based on source or destination IP, port, and protocol. They are stateful and rule-ordered; the first matching rule takes effect. A typical configuration allows management traffic only from a jump box IP and allows outbound connections to required Azure service endpoints. For example, you might permit inbound TCP port 22 only from your admin jump box, and permit outbound HTTPS to storage endpoints. A common error is relying solely on NSGs without a centralized firewall; NSGs are effective for subnet-level controls but they do not provide FQDN filtering or threat intelligence. Use NSGs for low-latency packet filtering and Azure Firewall when you need central policy, FQDN controls, or cross-VNet rules. When you design rules, document the justification and expiration for any wide-open rules; temporary allowances often become permanent if not audited. Consider how NSGs and route tables interact, and test rules in a staging VNet before applying to production. Network Security Groups (NSGs) — filtering traffic means use nsgs for targeted allow/deny controls and pair them with a centralized firewall when you need fqdn filtering or policy across vnets.. In practical terms, how nsgs enforce subnet- and vm-level rules. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Azure Firewall and NSGs complement each other but serve different needs. NSGs are efficient, low-latency packet filters used for subnet- or NIC-level access controls. They are rule-ordered and ideal for basic allow/deny scenarios. Azure Firewall is a managed, stateful, cloud firewall service that centralizes traffic policy across VNets and supports features NSGs do not: FQDN filtering, threat intelligence, and application rules that operate at the domain level. A practical design is to use NSGs to implement fast, layered filtering near compute and use Azure Firewall as a central enforcement point for egress policies and cross-VNet controls. For sensitive pipelines, Azure Firewall can block access to known malicious domains and allow lists of storage FQDNs, which NSGs cannot. A common misconception is to replace NSGs with Firewall entirely; instead, combine them: NSGs for local enforcement and Firewall for centralized policy and logging. Ask yourself: do you need domain-level control and threat intelligence, or only simple IP/port filtering? That question guides whether to add Firewall to your architecture. Azure Firewall vs NSGs means pair nsgs for local filtering with azure firewall for centralized, fqdn-aware egress control and threat intelligence.. In practical terms, when to use a centralized firewall and when nsgs are enough. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Azure Private Link enables private connectivity to PaaS services by presenting a Private Endpoint inside your VNet. That endpoint is a network interface assigned a private IP from your subnet, and it maps to the PaaS resource. The result: traffic flows over the Azure backbone and does not traverse the public internet. For data services like ADLS Gen2 or Azure S Q L, this means your data factory or Databricks cluster can access storage without hitting public endpoints. A concrete example is creating a Private Endpoint targeting the 'blob' or 'dfs' sub-resource of a storage account; once created and DNS is correctly configured, the storage FQDN resolves to the private IP. Common mistakes include leaving public access enabled after adding Private Link or failing to integrate a private DNS zone so resolution still returns public addresses. The important design idea is that Private Link removes exposure while preserving the managed PaaS experience. Think about how private endpoints affect peering, routing, and DNS when you plan subnet placement. Azure Private Link and Private Endpoints means private endpoints provide private ips for paas services so traffic stays on the azure backbone; dns integration is essential.. In practical terms, bringing paas services into your vnet with private ips. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

This walkthrough describes the conceptual steps to create a Private Endpoint for an ADLS Gen2 storage account. Follow these steps in your portal when you're ready. First, open the storage account and navigate to Networking, then choose Private Endpoint connections and add a new private endpoint. In Basics, pick subscription, resource group, name and region matching your VNet. Under Resource, select 'Connect to an Azure resource in my directory', set Resource type to Microsoft. Storage/storageAccounts, choose your storage account and target sub-resource 'blob' or 'dfs'. For Virtual Network, select the VNet and subnet where the endpoint's private IP will reside. The crucial DNS option is 'Integrate with private DNS zone' — set this to Yes to automatically create or link a privatelink DNS zone so your storage name resolves privately. Finally, review and create. A frequent misconception is proceeding without checking region and DNS; mismatched regions or missing private DNS integration will leave traffic resolving to public IPs. Remember: do not create a production endpoint without a plan for testing and cost review. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

When you create a Private Endpoint, DNS is the step that makes private connectivity usable. Private Link typically pairs a private endpoint with a private DNS zone such as privatelink. blob. core. windows. net. If you accept automatic integration, Azure will create or link the zone and add the appropriate A record so your storage account name resolves to the private IP. If you do not integrate DNS, clients inside your VNet will continue to see the public IP for the service and traffic will route through the public internet. A common pitfall is creating the Private Endpoint but failing to update DNS for peered VNets or on-premises resolver settings, leaving parts of the network still resolving publicly. For hybrid setups you may need conditional forwarders or DNS forwarding rules to ensure on-premises names resolve to private addresses. Always test resolution from the intended client host and verify that the fully qualified storage name maps to a private IP before disabling public access. Private DNS Zones and common DNS pitfalls means private endpoint creation is incomplete without private dns integration and resolver configuration for peered or on-prem clients.. In practical terms, ensure service names resolve to private ips inside your vnet. A concrete example makes the pattern visible, and a brief contrast helps prevent a common misconception. This matters because learners need the underlying reasoning before they can apply the idea confidently or notice where it breaks down. The main takeaway is that the concept should be understood as a meaningful pattern, not just a label on the screen.

Identity is the control plane that complements network isolation. Azure Active Directory is the identity provider for users, groups, service principals, and managed identities. Managed Identities are special identities assigned to Azure services so they can authenticate to resources without storing credentials.
